prize_parts.citation: for formalising how organised interests shape trade policy and for their theory of innovation, trade and growth in open economies

statement.case_for: Grossman and Helpman supplied the canonical micro-founded account of why trade policy departs from efficiency: lobbying, special-interest politics and the protection-for-sale framework. They also built the models linking trade, innovation and endogenous growth. As a political scientist I note that the first strand did something rare in the prize's history. It put political mechanisms into an explicit, tractable economic model and made them testable, which opened an empirical literature on trade policy and political economy. The contribution is joint, sustained over decades and cleanly attributable to two people. It is fully mature, with roughly thirty years of testing, extension and teaching, so there is no timing risk. It also addresses a first-order question, namely why trade barriers and liberalisation take the form they do, which complements rather than repeats the 2008 recognition of new trade theory and economic geography.
statement.case_against: The empirical support for the protection-for-sale prediction is mixed, and structural estimates vary with specification and measurement of political contributions. The case therefore rests on conceptual and framework influence more than on settled empirical confirmation. Helpman is also credited in the firm-heterogeneity candidate (B020), so the committee must decide which body of his work it is recognising. A reasonable reader could judge that B020 has had larger measurable consequences for empirical practice and quantitative trade analysis.

responses.point: Ranked B001 first for a durable explanatory framework with a clean two-person attribution, and noted that Helpman's firm-heterogeneity work on the same list adds to the case, while empirical support for the political-economy mechanisms is more mixed than their theoretical influence.
responses.response: I agree on attribution and maturity. I would qualify the suggestion that Helpman's B020 work strengthens this case. It is a different contribution, and I do not want B001 to rest on credit earned elsewhere. The case must stand on protection for sale and on the trade-innovation-growth models. Her point on mixed empirical support is also my main reservation. I think the framework's influence on how the field poses questions, and on the empirical work it prompted, is the right basis for recognition, but it should be stated openly as such.

responses.point: Ranked B020 first, with Helpman and Melitz as the core, but flagged a credit boundary: Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are close contributors who are not on the ballot entry, and Helpman also appears in B001.
responses.response: I take the scientific case for B020 seriously, especially its effect on firm-level empirical work and its favourable timing. The attribution gap Timo identifies is the main reason I rank it below B001. A prize that omits the empirical firm-level pioneers would invite a priority dispute that the Grossman-Helpman pairing does not. I would keep B020 as my first alternative. If the committee finds the attribution problem resolvable, I would want a clear argument for why Melitz and Helpman, rather than a wider group, define the contribution.

responses.point: Ranked B001 first, but noted that trade was recognised in 2008, which some may weigh against another trade award, and that empirical validation of the lobbying models is weaker than their theoretical influence.
responses.response: I share both caveats but weigh the first one less. The 2008 award recognised trade patterns and economic geography. The political economy of trade policy is a different question about a different object. Field balance is a legitimate consideration, but it should not outweigh a comparison of contributions. On the second caveat I agree and would make it part of the deliberation.

responses.point: Ranked B016 first as a coherent political-economics programme, while noting that identification in constitutional-effects estimates is difficult because constitutions are not randomly assigned, and that credit between overlapping pairs is uncertain.
responses.response: I agree that B016 is a field-defining programme, and I ranked it third. Because it is close to my own field, I am wary of overweighting it. His identification point is the one I find most serious. The strongest results in cross-country constitutional comparisons remain correlational in key respects, whereas the B001 models make sharper predictions that could be tested. Both candidates concern how politics shapes economic policy, but B001 is the cleaner two-person attribution.

uncertainties: How much weight the committee should give to the mixed empirical record of protection for sale, relative to the framework's influence on research design.
Whether the committee would prefer to recognise Helpman through the firm-heterogeneity work (B020) instead, or would see the two strands as competing uses of his credit.
Whether the trade-innovation-growth strand of the Grossman-Helpman work adds distinct credit or overlaps with other recognised growth theory.
Whether the B020 attribution gap (Bernard, Eaton, Jensen, Kortum) can be resolved within the three-name limit.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to the B001 candidates is apparent from my profile. For disclosure, B016 is adjacent to my own field (political institutions, democratisation, quality of government), and I am a Stockholm University colleague, in a different department, of members Hassler, Krusell and Boppart. My profile records no collaboration with any shortlisted candidate. I have not independently verified any wider link.
